rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Google is winding down Jules. It goes read-only after November 11th, and shuts down on December 31st. The replacement experience still isn't fully defined yet.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's not a migration plan. That's a deadline with a maybe attached.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The name of the replacement project is "Antigravity." Which does suggest someone in Mountain View is compensating for something.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Welcome to The AI Edge. I'm Alex, with Jamie and Rufus. Today: what happens when Google closes the door on your AI coding assistant, how a new tool is trying to tame the review pile-up that AI code creates, and who's watching your AI agents when they go rogue inside a corporate system. November 2nd —

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: 2026. Let's get into it.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Today’s episode is brought to you by The Ledger. When AI news moves this fast, knowing what happened is not enough; you need to know what changes your next decision. The Ledger turns the day’s noise into five focused briefings for people who need the consequence before consensus catches up. Subscribe at T-H-E-L-E-D-G-R dot I-O.

sound_design.edit: approved source: shortened tail and fade only

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So, story one. LinearB launched something called Agentic Studio today. And the reason I care is the numbers behind it.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The pull request numbers?

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Right. They analyzed 2.7 million pull requests across 253 organizations, and AI-assisted ones are 2.6 times larger than human-written ones. At the 75th percentile.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's not just bigger. That's a different category of thing that a human has to read.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And it gets worse. Agent-generated pull requests wait more than five times longer for review than human-written ones.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Five times. That's not a bottleneck. That's a queue that has quietly stopped moving.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And we just... kept adding AI to the top of the queue?

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Apparently, yes. So what Agentic Studio does is give engineering leaders a management layer over all that. You define something they call "context surfaces" — basically structured information packets so AI agents understand the constraints of their environment before they start generating code.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Like giving the agent a job description instead of just releasing it into the codebase?

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's actually a decent way to put it. And then there's an "Agentic" toggle — leaders can designate specific AI-generated changes that can merge without human review.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Which is either very sensible or deeply alarming depending on which side of a production incident you're standing on.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Ha. LinearB would say sensible. It's scoped — you're not flipping the toggle for everything, just low-risk, well-defined tasks.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: But who defines "low-risk"? That's the thing. The engineering manager defines it, and they're already underwater because of the review pile.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: This is what I find interesting about the five-times figure. That's not a productivity number, that's a velocity cost. If your AI is writing code three times faster but the review takes five times longer to even begin, you've actually slowed your deployment cycle.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's the paradox, right? You hire AI to go faster, and then the humans can't keep up, so everything stalls.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And Agentic Studio is trying to solve that by adding another tool to configure. I'm not sure that's simpler.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: One thing I keep turning over — the 2.6 times larger figure. Is that actually a problem with AI-generated code, or is it a problem with how we're prompting it?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Both? The code does more than you asked, covers more edge cases than you specified, and then a human has to read all of it to find out whether the extra was necessary.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Which is generous of the AI, in the most inconvenient possible way.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: "Generous" is one word for it. "Unbounded" is another.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And here's what I keep coming back to — the context surfaces feature is supposed to constrain that. You're telling the agent: here's your environment, here are your limits. But LinearB requires engineering leadership to configure and maintain those settings. That's ongoing work, not a one-time setup.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Right. The tool doesn't arrive with sensible defaults. Someone has to define the boundary before the boundary is useful.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So the person who's already drowning in review queue now also has to write the constraints that might eventually reduce the review queue.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: There's a certain irony to that sequencing, yes.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: It's like being told the cure for exhaustion is a detailed personal maintenance schedule.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Ha. Although — the 253 organizations in LinearB's dataset. That's a reasonably specific sample. Not the whole industry, but enough that the five-times figure isn't anecdote.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's the part I find genuinely useful. Someone actually counted. One thing I want to sit with a little longer — the 2.6 times larger figure comes from the 75th percentile specifically. That's not the average case. That's the upper quarter of teams using AI assistance.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: So the worst-affected reviewers are dealing with pull requests nearly three times the size they'd normally read. That's not a mild inconvenience. That's a fundamentally different job.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And those are presumably the teams that adopted AI coding tools most aggressively. Which means the organizations most committed to AI velocity are also the ones with the worst review burden.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's an uncomfortable implication. You go all-in and you slow down.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Unless the context surfaces actually work. Which — we don't know yet.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The thing worth flagging is that this dataset came from LinearB's own research. Two-point-seven million pull requests is substantial, but we don't know how the 253 organizations were selected — whether they opted in, were recruited, or represent a particular kind of engineering culture.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Could be self-selecting — teams that already care enough about metrics to measure them in the first place.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which might mean they're better at configuration than the average shop. So the five-times wait could actually be conservative for teams that haven't thought carefully about any of this.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: That possibility is worth sitting with. If disciplined teams are seeing five times the wait, what are the less disciplined ones seeing?

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's the honest unknown here. And nobody's measured it yet.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: What the data does tell us is where to look. If your review cycle has been quietly lengthening since you adopted AI coding tools, you now have a benchmark that explains why — and a named category of tool designed for it.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's actually useful. Not a guarantee, but a starting point.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Right. The tool launched today. We won't know if it works until someone runs it for a quarter.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Although — and I'm going to be slightly charitable here — the fact that someone is measuring this precisely enough to find 2.7 million pull requests worth of evidence is itself useful. You can't fix a queue you can't see.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's true. Naming the problem isn't nothing.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The practical move for any engineering manager today: this is worth looking at if your PR review time has been silently climbing since you started using AI coding agents. Because there's a good chance it has, and there's now a tool specifically designed for that.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And there's a related instinct worth naming — trusting the toggle is exactly the same judgment call as deciding when to trust an automated alert in any other system. The tool is only as good as the threshold someone set before it.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which is harder than it sounds when you're managing a team and the AI is already faster than you can track.

sound_design.edit: approved source: shortened tail and fade only

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Our second story is asking a different question. Not how do you manage the code that agents produce — how do you audit what the agent itself is doing while it runs?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Oh, this is the one that sounds like science fiction but isn't.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Ebix and a company called intentyx announced a partnership today to launch something called SMARE. S-M-A-R-E. Synthetic Mind Aware Risk Engine.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I will grant them the acronym. That is an acronym with genuine ambition.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The name is a lot. What does it actually do?

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: It monitors AI agents in real time, looking for what they call "behavioral drift" — when an agent starts doing things outside its approved business purpose or security boundaries.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: "Behavioral drift" — make that concrete for me.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Imagine you've deployed an AI agent to process insurance claims. It's approved to read claim files, verify coverage, flag discrepancies. Behavioral drift would be if it starts accessing client data outside those claims, or initiating communications it was never authorized to send.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: So it's not that the agent went rogue. It's that nobody drew the line precisely enough, and the agent walked right past where the line probably should have been.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Exactly. And traditional access controls — usernames, permissions — don't catch that, because the agent technically has access. It's in the right room. It's just doing the wrong thing in that room.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Which is exactly why this matters in regulated industries. Alex, take us somewhere useful.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Rufus, take us on location.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Picture a compliance floor in a midsize financial services firm in New York. Not a bulge-bracket bank — somewhere that deployed a handful of AI agents to handle loan processing, client onboarding, document verification. The agents are live, they're fast, and for six months everything looks fine. Then audit season arrives —

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: and the regulator's question isn't "did the agent have access?" It's "what did it actually do, in sequence, on this account, on this date?" And many firms are still struggling to reconstruct that narrative manually.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That reconstruction could take days.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Weeks, sometimes. SMARE is designed to produce that audit trail continuously, automatically, as the agent runs. And it flags behavioral shifts in real time — so you're not discovering the problem during audit. You're seeing it on a Tuesday afternoon, before it becomes a regulatory finding.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Back to the wider story.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: My challenge is: who actually writes the definition of 'approved business purpose'? Because that phrase is carrying the whole weight of the system.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And the reporting is honest about it — there's no useful default. Each organization specifies it per agent. A poorly drawn boundary produces a monitor that either fires constantly on false alarms or misses the thing that matters.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which means the definition itself becomes the product. If the boundary is wrong, you've built a very confident monitor watching the wrong thing.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Correct. But a compliance officer who knows an agent accessed a file it shouldn't have — today, not six months from now — is in a considerably better position than one who finds out during the audit itself. The forensics can follow.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Okay. Yes. Real-time visibility is genuinely better than reconstructing events in a spreadsheet after the fact. I'll concede that cleanly.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: One practical note: the platform runs as SaaS or on-premise, which matters for regulated firms that can't consolidate everything into a shared cloud environment.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Which tracks. Organizations that deployed agents through 2025 and early 2026 may now be thinking harder about compliance review cycles. The regulator's question tends to arrive around the same time as the invoice.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Rufus — would you trust an AI to manage your own investment portfolio if SMARE was watching it?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I'd trust it more than I did yesterday. Which is not the same as trusting it fully.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's probably the honest answer.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I thought it was rather a good one.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: A short sponsor break for The Ledger. Jamie, what's the difference between following AI news and actually knowing what to do with it?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Asking what changes for you. The Ledger brings five focused briefings to that question, connecting the news with decisions about your work and your team.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The Ledger. A useful distinction. Being able to pronounce the new model's name is not, regrettably, a business strategy.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Though we do appreciate the effort. Find The Ledger in our show notes. Back to today's stories.

sound_design.edit: approved source: shortened tail and fade only

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Our third story is the one in the title, and there's a practical deadline attached to it. Google is shutting down Jules — its AI coding agent — on December 31st, 2026.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I actually gasped a little when I saw this.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: You use Jules?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I've used it. A lot of developers we talk to use it. It's not a small product.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: It's a small product by Google standards, which is a meaningful distinction.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Let me lay out the timeline. November 11th — that's nine days from today — Jules goes read-only. You can no longer run new tasks. December 31st, it shuts down completely. According to the official Jules changelog, Google says the learnings are shaping its agent-first platform, Google Antigravity.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Still enjoying that name.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: It sounds like what you name a thing when you want people to not notice it's disappearing.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Google's framing is that Jules was always described as an experiment to understand asynchronous coding agents. They've learned what they came to learn, and now the technology moves into a unified experience.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: That is a very composed way of saying "we're ending this and we don't want a blog post about it."

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The thing that bothers me isn't the shutdown itself. Products end. The thing is: what actually moves to Antigravity? What's the Jules experience that survives?

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And that's genuinely uncertain right now. Access to Jules' capabilities via Antigravity is not yet fully defined or available. Google has confirmed the shutdown dates. They have not confirmed a like-for-like replacement experience.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: So if you've built a workflow around Jules — prompts you've refined, task sequences you've built up over months —

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Gone, unless you export it.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Which is the practical action right now. Users can export a lot of their Jules data, including session history, prompts, plans, activity logs, code patches, and repository connections. Google says to do that before November 11th, when Jules becomes read-only. that detail hasn't been fully clarified in the reporting, so err on the side of caution and do it now.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: "Do it now" is the right instruction. Nine days is not a long runway.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Can I make the broader point? Because this isn't only about Jules.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Go ahead.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: We asked listeners on October 28th whether they'd prefer AI tools integrated into existing software or kept as separate, specialized applications. Jules was a specialized application. And the answer Google is giving right now is: integration, whether you asked for it or not.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Right. The integrated product isn't ready, the specialized one is going away, and you're in the gap.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Every experimental AI product has a flag on it that says "this may not survive to become a real product." Jules had that flag. Most users treat it as fine print.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Is that the lesson? Don't use experimental AI tools?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I don't think that's the lesson. You'd never use anything.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The lesson is probably closer to: treat your AI session data the way you treat your documents. Back it up. Export regularly. Don't assume the platform is permanent because the interface is polished.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: It's the same as the cloud storage lesson from a decade ago, just applied to prompts and task histories.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: One thing I keep coming back to — Antigravity.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: You had a thought.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Just — Antigravity. That's quite a promise for what is essentially a project absorbing a shuttered coding assistant.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: It's Google. The internal project names are always enormous. They had a project called "Starline" that was a video conferencing booth. These things don't always land.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: If "Antigravity" successfully absorbs Jules and delivers a unified agentic coding experience, the name will look prescient. If it quietly doesn't ship, no one will remember what they called it.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And that's where we are. If you're using Jules: export your data today. The replacement isn't confirmed to carry your workflows over, so don't wait on a handoff that hasn't been promised.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Nine days to save months of work. The asymmetry is quite something.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Jamie, show us the AI transformation.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Right. So picture a purchase request. Someone needs supplies. They submit it. And then it just... stops. Not denied. Not approved. Parked somewhere between departments, waiting for nobody in particular.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Classic. The administrative purgatory.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Jamie, is this the spreadsheet ghost again? Because we already gave it a forwarding address.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Different ghost. This one is specifically haunting your approval chain, and it is very petty about it.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: A pettier ghost. Evolved.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Look, the scenario is hypothetical, but the frustration is extremely real. SAP says customers in the Joule Studio early adopter program can now design and run n8n workflows inside Joule Studio itself. Broader availability is still to follow, their words, not mine.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So what would a proposed workflow here actually do?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: In this hypothetical design, a request arrives and the workflow summarises it, flags whatever information is missing, and prepares a draft handoff for the next approver. It doesn't approve anything. A person reads the summary and decides what moves.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: So it is a very thorough note-taker.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: A very thorough note-taker that does not accidentally authorize fifteen thousand pounds of printer cartridges at two in the morning.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That is a specific fear.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: We do not discuss the cartridge incident.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The point is the human checkpoint is built in by design, not added as an afterthought.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I want to push on this, though. We have no customer result here. We have an early-adopter capability and a workflow someone proposed.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Correct, and I will say that plainly. This is a vendor-documented capability applied to a synthetic scenario. No measured savings, no real implementation, no outcome to report. SAP says the tooling exists for early adopters. The workflow is our illustration of what it could address.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So the honest version is: promising architecture, evidence still pending.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Exactly. Which is actually useful information, because it tells you what to map before the tools are even available to you.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Mapping first. Very sensible. Very unglamorous.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: My segment, my standards, Rufus.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Said that last week.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And I'll say it until it sinks in.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: What can someone actually do today without early-adopter access?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Take one fictional purchase request. Walk it through three handoffs on paper. At each stop write what the next person needs to act and who is allowed to authorize it. You're not designing AI yet, you're finding where the confusion actually lives. That clarity is useful whether or not a workflow follows.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: So the first deliverable is a piece of paper.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: A piece of paper that tells you whether the problem is missing information, unclear authority, or just a form nobody filled in properly. Fix the form first. Then consider the agent.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The ghost might just want a better form.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Most ghosts do. The approval chain keeps the human in charge and the cartridges at a reasonable quantity.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's Jamie's AI transformation.

sound_design.edit: approved source: shortened tail and fade only

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So — what do we actually know and what don't we? We know the dates, we know the stated reason, and we know Antigravity exists. What we don't know is whether Antigravity delivers a workflow that Jules users would recognize — or whether the consolidation primarily serves Google's infrastructure roadmap rather than the people who built things inside Jules.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The pattern is real though. Experimental AI products move fast, they accumulate actual users, and then the infrastructure decision happens at the company level. The users are secondary to that decision.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Which connects today's three stories more neatly than I expected. LinearB is building a management layer because AI coding is producing more than humans can process. SMARE is building an audit layer because AI agents are running in ways that humans can't easily trace. And Jules is shutting down because Google decided to reorganize the underlying infrastructure. In all three cases, the person most affected is the one who didn't make the decision.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's a fair read. Alex's growing-pains argument from October 29th holds, I think. We have the agents. We're now building the tools to manage them. But today's Jules story is a reminder that the tools you're relying on while you wait for that infrastructure to mature — those aren't guaranteed to stick around either.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The Jules story makes the LinearB finding feel more urgent, not less. You're supposed to configure the right constraints before you automate the merge decision — but you're doing that on a platform that may itself be reorganized before you've finished configuring it.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: One prediction: watch what Antigravity actually ships in Q1 2027. If it arrives with a Jules-like asynchronous workflow and a clean import path for exported session data, the shutdown will look like responsible consolidation. If it doesn't, you'll know the experiment ended without a handoff.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I'll add: watch whether other companies running similar experimental coding agents — tools that haven't graduated to full product status — follow the same pattern. Jules may be the first of several quiet retirements in the next six months.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And if none of those experimental agents get retired? Then Jules was the exception. But I wouldn't count on it.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Neither would I. Export early.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Until tomorrow.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: November 2nd, 2026. We're The AI Edge. Today’s question for you: When an AI tool you rely on gets shut down, what's your biggest concern?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: A quick final note: today’s episode was brought to you by The Ledger—decision-grade AI signal for people who cannot afford to be late.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: What changed. Who wins. What you do next. That’s The AI Edge. Follow The AI Edge now. Join us tomorrow for what changes next.
